title: Which problem first
objectives: Choose the order of problems by points and difficulty.

screens.title: Which first?
screens.prose: A two-hour round with decaying scores. Our rule: a problem loses $v / 250$ points a minute until solved, 50 per rejected attempt, and never falls below $0.3v$. You estimate each problem's solving time. These numbers are this course's illustration; check a real round's announcement for its rule.

screens.title: One score
screens.prose: Our rule: a problem loses $v / 250$ points a minute until solved, 50 per rejected attempt, and never falls below $0.3v$. You solve B (1,000 points) at minute 35, after one rejected attempt.
screens.question: What does B score?

hints.text: Start from 1,000 and take off the minutes, then the attempt.
B loses $1000 / 250 = 4$ points a minute.
$1000 - 4 \cdot 35 - 50 = 810$, above the floor of 300.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 4 per minute and 50 per rejected attempt.

byKey.nopen: You left out the rejected attempt, which costs 50.
byKey.floor: The floor is 300, but 810 is above it, so it does not apply.
byKey.twice: You charged the attempt twice. One rejection costs 50.

explain.text: Thirty-five minutes cost 140 points and the rejection 50, so B scores 810. In a two-hour round, time alone takes at most 48% of a problem's value. So the floor of 30% is reached only when rejections add to the cost.

screens.title: The score as code
screens.prose: Write `decayed_score(value, minute, wrong, per_minute, per_wrong, floor)`. It is the larger of `floor * value` and the value less the time and attempt costs. Here `floor` is a fraction such as 0.3.
screens.question: Write `decayed_score`.

widget.starter:
def decayed_score(value, minute, wrong, per_minute, per_wrong, floor):
    ...
widget.solution:
def decayed_score(value, minute, wrong, per_minute, per_wrong, floor):
    return max(floor * value, value - per_minute * minute - per_wrong * wrong)
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests on the rule above. They include A late with three rejections, where the floor applies, and the floor reached exactly at minute 175. Test 7 has a floor of 0. Answers are compared within $10^{-9}$.

hints.text: Two candidates; return the larger.
One is `floor * value`.
`return max(floor * value, value - per_minute * minute - per_wrong * wrong)`.

feedback.correct: The decayed value, floored at a fraction of the original.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is A at minute 120 with three rejections: $500 - 240 - 150 = 110$, below the floor of 150. Apply the floor after both costs.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has a floor of 0 and a value that decays below 0. The floor still holds: the score is 0.

explain.text: Taking the larger of the two applies the floor after both costs. Test 5 sits exactly on it: $1000 - 4 \cdot 175 = 300 = 0.3 \cdot 1000$.

screens.title: ICPC-style ranking
screens.prose: An ICPC-style round ranks by problems solved, then by penalty, lower first. A solved problem's penalty is its solve minute plus 20 per rejected attempt (our illustration). Write `icpc_rank_key(results)` returning `(-solved, penalty)`. Each result is `(minute or None, wrong)`.

tests.call: [t for t, r in sorted(teams, key=lambda tr: icpc_rank_key(tr[1]))]

D is unsolved, so its three rejections do not count.

feedback.correct: Solved count first, then penalty from solved problems only.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `(-3, 208)`. D's three rejections do not count, because D was never solved.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 is a solve at minute 0 after five rejections. Test `minute is not None`: a bare `if minute:` drops a solve at minute 0.

screens.title: Forty-five minutes on D
screens.prose: Eighty minutes into a two-hour round, you have spent 45 minutes on D. It has two rejections and you have no new idea. C, worth 1,500, is unread.

screens.question: What do you do now?

options.text: Move to C now; return to D only with a new idea
Stay on D, or the 45 minutes are wasted

options.text: Resubmit D with a small change and hope

C needs about 30 minutes and has not lost its chance.

feedback.correct: Move on: the spent time is gone either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge only the time that is left.

byKey.stay: You stayed because of the time already spent. That is the sunk-cost mistake; the 45 minutes are gone either way.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trust the solve counts over the letters.

byKey.l5: You followed the letters. Only 96 have solved D, against 702 for E.

explain.text: Letters are the setters' guess; the scoreboard is thousands of contestants' evidence. Here the hardest-lettered problem is the easier one.

screens.title: Why points per minute
screens.prose:
Take neighbouring problems $i$ and $j$. Doing $i$ first, $j$ waits $t_i$ minutes and loses $v_j t_i / 250$. Doing $j$ first, $i$ loses $v_i t_j / 250$. So $i$ first loses

$$\frac{v_j t_i - v_i t_j}{250}$$

more points while neither score is at its floor. That is negative exactly when $v_i / t_i > v_j / t_j$.
screens.question: How many more points does C then D score than D then C?

hints.text: Take $i = $ C and $j = $ D.
$v_D t_C - v_C t_D = 2000 \cdot 35 - 1500 \cdot 50$.

feedback.correct: 20 points: C then D scores more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put C's and D's values into the formula.

byKey.neg: −20 is the change in points *lost*. Losing 20 fewer means scoring 20 more.
byKey.big: You forgot to divide by 250, the rate rule's denominator.

explain.text: A B C D scores 3,550 and A B D C scores 3,530: the swap costs 20. This is lesson 10's exchange argument applied to the round itself.

screens.title: The best order, by brute force
screens.prose: Write `best_order(problems, minutes)`. Each problem is `(name, value, time)`; solve them back to back. Use `decayed_score(value, finish, 0, value / 250, 50, 0.3)`, and a problem finishing after `minutes` scores 0. Return `(total, names)` for the best order. On a tie, return the alphabetically first order.
screens.question: Write `best_order`.

widget.prelude:
def decayed_score(value, minute, wrong, per_minute, per_wrong, floor):

Then a problem that cannot finish, two problems, and six problems in 180 minutes (720 orders). `decayed_score` is already defined. Answers are compared exactly. The result is only as good as the time estimates.

hints.text: Six problems give at most 720 orders: try them all.
Sort the problems by name first, so `permutations` gives orders alphabetically.
For each order, add each finish time and score it if it is within `minutes`. Keep an order only if its total is strictly larger.

feedback.correct: Every order tried, ties broken alphabetically.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 has only 60 minutes. No three problems fit, and B then C is worth 2,090.

screens.title: Triage on a desk
screens.prose: Half an hour before the close, three tasks wait on a trading desk. Each has an estimated value and time, and loses a fixed share of its value each minute it waits. The same rule applies: value per minute, largest first.
screens.question: Which task first?

options.text: Hedge the position: the largest value
options.why: You chose the biggest value. At £480 a minute it is second; the quote earns £600 a minute.

options.text: Reconcile the break: clear the oldest problem first
options.why: You chose by age. At £100 a minute it comes last.

hints.text: Divide value by minutes for each task.
Quote £600, hedge £480, reconcile £100 a minute: quote first, then the hedge.

feedback.correct: Quote first, then the hedge; the break waits until after the close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare value per minute.

byKey.hedge: You chose by size. The quote takes 5 minutes and earns more per minute, then the hedge still fits.

explain.text: Both fit in the half hour, so only the waiting differs. At 1% a minute, quote first costs the hedge £600 and hedge first costs the quote £750. If an interview sets three questions in an hour, the same habit helps: bank the quick one, then go deep.

ideas: Read every statement, then solve in order of points per minute: value over estimated time, largest first.
Cap the time on a stuck problem: the spent minutes are gone, and resubmitting without a new idea only adds penalties.
The scoreboard beats the letters: many solves of a later problem mean it is easier.

quiz.prose: Under our rule, a 1,000-point problem loses 4 points a minute and 50 per rejection. Its floor is 30%. You solve it at minute 180 after one rejection.
quiz.question: What does it score?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the decayed value, then compare it with the floor.

byKey.nofloor: 230 is below the floor, and the score never falls below $0.3 \cdot 1000 = 300$.
byKey.nopen: 280 leaves out the rejection, and it is below the floor anyway: the score is 300.

quiz.prose: ICPC style, 20 penalty minutes per rejection on a solved problem. X solved at 15, 50 and 90, with two rejections on the second. Y solved at 20, 45 and 100, with one rejection on the third. Z solved four problems.
quiz.question: What is the ranking?

options.why: You ranked X above Y. X's penalty is $155 + 40 = 195$ and Y's is $165 + 20 = 185$, so Y is ahead.

options.text: Y, X, then Z: Z's times are later
options.why: You ranked by penalty first. More solves always rank higher.

feedback.correct: Solves first, then the lower penalty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count solves, then add the penalties.

explain.text: Z's four solves beat any three. X: $15 + 50 + 90 + 2 \cdot 20 = 195$; Y: $20 + 45 + 100 + 20 = 185$. So Y ranks above X.

quiz.prose: P is worth 750 and takes about 25 minutes. Q is worth 1,250 and takes about 50.
quiz.question: Which do you solve first?

options.why: You chose by value alone. Q earns 25 points a minute and P 30.

options.text: Either: the total is the same
options.why: The order changes how long each problem waits, so the totals differ.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare points per minute.

explain.text: $750 / 25 = 30$ and $1250 / 50 = 25$. So P goes first, which is also the order `best_order` finds for this pair.

quiz.prose: You have spent 30 minutes on a problem and have no new idea. Thirty minutes are left, and two unread problems remain.
quiz.question: Which reason for staying is a good one?

options.text: You have a new idea for the rejected case
You have already put 30 minutes in
options.why: You chose the time already spent. It is gone whatever you do next.
A feeling without a new idea usually means another rejection. Read the unread problems first.

feedback.correct: Only a new idea justifies staying.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which reason is about the next 30 minutes.

explain.text: Staying is right only when the next minutes on this problem beat the alternatives. A concrete new idea is evidence of that; time already spent is not.
